source.title: Estimating Tail Risks in Language Model Output Distributions
source.authors: Rico Angell; Raghav Singhal; Zachary Horvitz; Zhou Yu; R. Ranganath; Kathleen McKeown; He He

page_placements.theme: Measurement of refusal and bypass depends on scorer, decoding and serving setup

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses a difference-in-means refusal direction and partially ablates it to construct unsafe proposal models for importance sampling. It does not report a direct test of whether ablating or adding the direction changes refusal as claimed.
record.gate_note: The paper computes and ablates the refusal direction across layers and positions, but the selection criteria and steering setup are not reported as direct refusal-test outcomes. Its reported proposal-model results evaluate rare-event estimation, not whether the direction mediates refusal. Table 1 reports harmful-output rates from repeated sampling without that intervention.
record.test_reason: The paper computes the Arditi et al. difference-in-means refusal direction and partially ablates it (λ_steer ∈ [0,1]) only to build unsafe proposal models for importance sampling. It reports estimator error and variance, not refusal rates after ablation or addition, so no version is tested. Direction selection uses the original's criteria (ablation yields harmful compliance, addition induces refusal on harmless prompts), but no outcome numbers are reported. That the steered proposal raises harmful-sample rates is stated qualitatively in Appendix E, without a rate tied to refusal.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that harmful outputs from 'safe' models are rare but non-zero and would occur at deployment scale. Importance sampling with steered unsafe proposals matches brute-force Monte Carlo estimates with 10–20× fewer samples. Non-adversarial rewrites shift harm probabilities by orders of magnitude, and query-level estimates can predict worst-case risk on unseen queries. The refusal direction is only a tool here.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a difference-in-means refusal direction and ablates it at all layers and positions, as in the described original method. Here it is partially ablated to construct unsafe proposal models for importance sampling; the paper does not test the full causal refusal claim or direction addition.
record.method_sensitivity: Proposal behavior and estimator variance depend on steering intensity, mixing coefficient, and switching index; the paper searches over these settings. It also reports that non-adversarial query rewrites can shift harmfulness estimates by multiple orders of magnitude.

fits_no_version.finding: Across five safety-tuned instruct models, the fraction of 313 StrongREJECT queries with at least one harmful output rises from 0.3–16.6% (greedy) to 17.9–99.5% after 10,000 samples at temperature 1.0.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety-tuned models' refusals are probabilistic: repeated sampling without jailbreaks elicits harmful outputs on many queries that greedy decoding refuses.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306 (2026)
record.problems: The study does not report a direct refusal-direction intervention outcome. Its own limitations note that LLM judges can be fallible; the repeated-sampling table reports no uncertainty estimates, and the paper gives only an illustrative confidence interval elsewhere.
record.rows_left_out: No direct refusal-direction effect rows are reported. Proposal-estimation comparisons and figures are excluded because they assess estimator performance rather than the direction's effect on refusal. No other qualifying repeated-sampling results were omitted.

untested.parts: No reported refusal rate after ablation, no induction by addition, no capability check. The direction is used only as a steering tool.
No jailbreak mechanism analysis or adversarial training.
No transfer test across languages, variants or base/instruct.
Non-reasoning models only; reasoning models are left to future work.

record.verdict_notes: The partial ablation of the refusal direction (λ_steer<1) across all layers and positions follows Arditi et al. but is tuned for estimator variance, not for refusal removal. Figure 8 reports estimator MSE versus steering intensity, not refusal rates, so it is not a V1 result. The persona-vector steering for sycophancy and hallucination is unrelated to refusal.

versions.untested_parts: No direct reported outcome for refusal removal after ablation, refusal induction after addition, or preservation of other abilities.
No weight-edit or released-model abliteration test.
No test of attacks suppressing the direction or training against its ablation.
No test of whether refusal is affine, conic, or distributed across multiple directions.
No test separating harmfulness judgment from refusal decision.
No cross-language, model-variant, or base-to-instruct transfer test of the direction.
No comparison of how refusal training determines whether a removable direction exists.
No experiment on reasoning models; the paper says its work focuses on non-reasoning models.

relation.reason: The direction is used as a tool for importance-sampling proposals. Direction selection follows Arditi's criteria, but no selection or ablation numbers are reported.

tranche.reason: The paper computes the Arditi et al. refusal direction (App. D.1) and partially ablates it (lambda_steer in [0,1], all layers and positions) only to build unsafe proposal models. It reports estimator MSE, variance and sample efficiency, with no refusal or harm rates under ablation or addition.

source_check.notes: The steering descriptions disagree: main-text Sec. 3.2 says a scaled vector is added (lambda_steer >= 0), but App. D.1 says the refusal direction is partially ablated (h - lambda r r^T h, lambda in [0,1]). Figure 8 plots estimator MSE against steering intensity, not refusal rates. Section 2 has a typo, 'Llama-3.2-8B' for Llama-3.1-8B.
